Original response headers dropped on JSON pass-through
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Original response headers dropped on JSON pass-through**

When the body is already valid JSON (the error pass-through path), the response is reconstructed using `res.headers` — but `res.headers` is the original `Headers` object from the consumed `Response`. At this point `res.body` has already been consumed via `res.text()`, so re-using `res.headers` is fine for the headers themselves. However, if the original response set a `content-type` other than `application/json` (e.g. `text/plain` for some proxy errors), the caller receives a body that is JSON but labelled otherwise. This is a minor inconsistency but could confuse downstream content-type checks.

claims.title: `parseCodexSSEResponse` silently drops unrecognised SSE event types
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**`parseCodexSSEResponse` silently drops unrecognised SSE event types**

The loop only processes `response.output_item.done` and `response.completed` — every other event type is silently discarded. That is intentional for normal operation, but if the API changes event names (e.g. renames `response.output_item.done` to something else), the function will return `{ ...finalResponse, output: [] }` with an empty output array and no warning. This is the exact bug the PR is fixing on the *input* side (`response.completed.output` was silently empty); the fix should not replicate the same silent-empty-array pattern on its output side. A `console.warn` or similar when `outputItems` is empty after parsing a non-empty stream would make this detectable.

Error response headers stripped when re-wrapping plain JSON
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Error response headers stripped when re-wrapping plain JSON**

When a plain-JSON response passes through (the `JSON.parse` succeeds branch), the re-wrapped `Response` is constructed with `headers: res.headers`. However, for the SSE success path, only `{ "content-type": "application/json" }` is set, which is correct. But in the error pass-through branch the original `Content-Type` header is preserved — which is fine — yet any other headers (e.g. `Retry-After`, `X-Request-Id`) are also preserved, which is the desired behaviour. This is actually correct as written; however, there is a subtle asymmetry: the SSE branch *drops* all original response headers (e.g. request-id headers useful for debugging). Consider spreading original headers and only overriding `content-type` in the SSE branch so tracing headers are preserved.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
return new Response(JSON.stringify(parsedResponse), {
				status: res.status,
				statusText: res.statusText,
				headers: { ...Object.fromEntries(res.headers.entries()), "content-type": "application/json" },
			});
```

**Error body truncated to 200 chars may hide relevant SSE events in real failures**

**JSDoc @param wraps mid-sentence, breaking rendered output**

claims.title: CRLF normalization applied only to block splitting, not to per-line parsing inside blocks
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**CRLF normalization applied only to block splitting, not to per-line parsing inside blocks**

The `.replace(/
/g, "
")` is applied before `.split("

")`, which fixes block boundary splitting. However, within each block the code later does `line.startsWith("data: ")` and `line.startsWith("event: ")` line-by-line splits. If a block internally contains `
`-separated lines (possible after only normalizing the double-newline separator), those inner lines would still carry a trailing ``, causing `line.startsWith("event: response.output_item.done")` to match but `line.slice(6)` to produce JSON with a trailing `` that breaks `JSON.parse`. The fix must normalize `rawSSEText` entirely before any splitting, which the current patch does — but only if `
` is used consistently. A stream that uses `
` within a block but `

` between blocks (malformed but possible) would still fail. Since the normalization is applied to the whole string before any split, the common case is handled correctly; this is a low-severity edge case.

claims.title: Normalization discards `\r` that is not part of a `\r\n` pair
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Normalization discards `\r` that is not part of a `\r\n` pair**

The normalization `rawSSEText.replace(/\r\n/g, "\n")` only converts `\r\n` → `\n`. A lone `\r` (old Mac-style line ending) is left in the string and will be included in the field value after splitting on `\n`. This is unlikely to occur from the Codex backend in practice, but if a proxy or CDN ever translates line endings to CR-only, field values will contain a trailing `\r` that silently corrupts the parsed JSON (the `data:` prefix strip leaves `{...}\r` which `JSON.parse` will reject). Consider using `rawSSEText.replace(/\r\n|\r/g, "\n")` to also normalize lone `\r`.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
	// The real backend uses LF-only (confirmed live), but SSE permits CRLF or bare CR —
	// normalize first so a server that does isn't silently misparsed.
	const blocks = rawSSEText
		.replace(/\r\n|\r/g, "\n")
		.split("\n\n")
		.filter((b) => b.trim());
```

claims.title: CRLF normalization now strips bare `\r` that may be legitimate content
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**CRLF normalization now strips bare `` that may be legitimate content**

The replacement `/
|/g` converts bare `` to `
`, which changes the meaning of any data payload that legitimately contains a carriage return not followed by `
`. The SSE spec (RFC 8895 §9.2) recognises only `
`, ``, and `
` as line terminators, so treating bare `` as a line terminator is correct for *line-splitting purposes* — but the current code applies the substitution before splitting, which means a `data:` value such as `data: foobar` becomes two lines (`data: foo` and `bar`) rather than one. The practical impact on the Codex backend is low because its payloads are JSON objects (no bare `` inside them), but the logic is subtly wrong and will silently corrupt any future payload that contains one.

A safer approach: normalise only `
` → `
` for block/line splitting, and strip a trailing `` from each parsed line value rather than replacing all bare `` upfront.

claims.title: Inner catch rethrows a new Error, dropping the original error's stack and type
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Inner catch rethrows a new Error, dropping the original error's stack and type**

The `catch (parseErr)` block constructs a brand-new `Error` and passes `parseErr` as `cause`. While `cause` is preserved (which is good — this was a prior finding), the rethrown error's own stack trace starts at this line, not at the site in `parseCodexSSEResponse` where parsing actually failed. For a `medium`-severity parse failure that only shows up in production logs, the `cause.stack` is easy to overlook. This is the same structural issue that was already on record; the `{ cause: parseErr }` addition in this diff partially mitigates it but does not fully resolve it since callers that log only `err.message` still lose the original location.

claims.title: Bare \r normalization may silently corrupt data in non-CRLF contexts
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Bare \r normalization may silently corrupt data in non-CRLF contexts**

The replacement `rawSSEText.replace(/\r\n|\r/g, "\n")` converts bare `\r` (carriage return not followed by `\n`) to `\n`. In the SSE context this is almost certainly correct per RFC, but if any SSE event data payload legitimately contains a bare `\r` (e.g. a JSON string value with `\r`), it will be silently mutated before parsing. The JSON payload itself is also normalized, not just the framing. This can corrupt embedded string values that contain `\r` characters. A safer approach is to normalize only framing characters (the blank-line separators and line prefixes) rather than the raw text wholesale.

The catch block constructs `new Error(…, { cause: parseErr })` which is now in the diff, so the chain is preserved. **cause normalization wraps a non-Error into a new Error before throwing, dropping the original**

The new `cause` normalization correctly boxes non-Error thrown values, but then throws `{ cause }` — meaning if `parseErr` was originally an `Error`, `cause === parseErr` (good), but if it was a string or number, the new wrapping `Error` is both the `cause` and has a `.message` equal to `String(parseErr)`. For the common case where `parseErr` is an `Error` this is identical to the previous behavior, so the risk is low, but the comment claims `cause` is "consistently typed" which is only partially true: a non-Error `parseErr` produces a wrapping Error whose own `cause` is `undefined`, not the original value.

claims.text:

**Bare \r normalization may silently corrupt non-CRLF carriage returns**

The replacement `rawSSEText.replace(/\r\n/g, "\n")` (visible in the prior diff context) is correct for CRLF streams. However, if an earlier round also introduced a bare-`\r` strip (replacing lone `\r` not preceded by `\n`), that would silently discard carriage returns that appear legitimately in base64-encoded or binary-safe event payloads. The JSDoc now mentions bare-CR normalization but the implementation comment says it is 'confirmed live' as LF-only, making the bare-CR branch untested and potentially data-corrupting. If bare-CR normalization is retained, add a test that verifies a `\r`-only delimiter produces the same output as `\n`; if it is not needed, remove the branch and update the JSDoc.

The new test for the error-status pass-through path uses `{ "retry-after": "30" }` as the only header, which cannot catch the bug where `content-encoding` is forwarded on a decoded body. Adding a `content-encoding: identity` (or `gzip`) header to the fixture and asserting it is absent (or present but harmless) on the returned Response would cover the regression identified above.

claims.title: Error-status pass-through reconstructs a new Response from `rawText`, but the original body was already consumed
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Error-status pass-through reconstructs a new Response from `rawText`, but the original body was already consumed**

When `res.ok` is false and `parseCodexSSEResponse` throws, the code returns `new Response(rawText, ...)` where `rawText` was obtained by `await res.text()` earlier. This is correct — `rawText` is already a string in scope, so the body is not double-consumed here. However, passing `res.headers` directly into the new `Response` constructor may not work as expected in all environments: `Response` headers are copied by value in the Fetch API, but `res.headers` is the original `Headers` object from the upstream response. This is safe in Node.js/undici and browsers, so this is not a blocking concern — just worth noting that the headers reference is shared rather than cloned.

More importantly: the test at line 330 now correctly validates that error-status responses pass through with `status`, `statusText`, and `headers` intact. This is a genuine improvement over the previous `throw`-on-all-parse-failures path.

claims.title: Success-status parse failure still discards `res.headers` from the upstream response
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Success-status parse failure still discards `res.headers` from the upstream response**

When `res.ok` is true and `parseCodexSSEResponse` throws, the code throws a new `Error` — the original `res.headers` (which may contain rate-limit, trace-ID, or retry headers) are lost. This is a narrower case than before (only 2xx responses that are neither JSON nor SSE trigger this path), but if a 200 response carries a `retry-after` header on a transient parse failure, that information is gone. replies.body: **No change —** the described corruption can't actually occur here. A `data:` line's payload is JSON, and RFC 8259 §7 requires control characters (including a raw CR, U+000D) to be escaped inside a JSON string — a conforming producer never emits a literal \r byte inside `data: {...}`; it would already be invalid JSON either way, blanket-replaced or not. The SSE-framing-level observation (CR alone is a valid line terminator per the spec) is correct, but it doesn't create a real corruption risk for this specific JSON-only payload. Asking the wrapper to somehow preserve the inner stack as if it were the outer error's own stack isn't how `Error.cause` works anywhere in the ecosystem — that would require re-throwing the original error, which loses the outer, more specific diagnostic message entirely.
